MEMBRANE: Illustrative harmonic frequencies 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 Hz are intentionally assigned for teaching, as requested; they are not the natural eigenfrequencies of this rectangular membrane. The animation and mode labels use those same frequencies, uniformly slowed by 250. Modal coefficients are 0.55/abs(phi_mn(pickup)), giving five equal-height measured spectral peaks at the marked point. The aspect ratio Lx/Ly=1.15; shapes are (1,1),(2,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,1), with phi_mn=sin(m*pi*x/Lx)sin(n*pi*y/Ly). All edges are fixed. The pickup is (x/Lx,y/Ly)=(0.23,0.31). Combined surface is vertically reduced to fit, at 0.057/0.24 of the magnification used in individual panels. The combined field is the exact sum of the five illustrated motions.

Clicking the video can pause/resume it. Static thumbnails and document previews show only the poster frame. The demonstration repeats every 60 seconds.

FIXED–FREE STRING: s=0 at bottom and s=L at top. phi_j(s)=sin((2j-1)*pi*s/(2L)), j=1..4. The displacement vanishes at the bottom; the spatial derivative vanishes at the top, which is a displacement antinode. Frequencies 100,300,500,700 Hz are shown at 0.4,1.2,2.0,2.8 Hz (1/250 speed). Equal modal coefficients give equal spectral peaks for the four-mode mixture measured at the free end. The four panels show the modes separately. The ideal free transverse boundary can be realized by a frictionless sliding endpoint while maintaining tension. These are separately tuned examples: for identical length and wave speed, changing a fixed–fixed string to fixed–free halves its fundamental; setting both examples to 100 Hz implies retuning length or wave speed.

When we compress air, as happens in a constriction, its stiffness rises, so making a constriction at a place that experiences lots of compression, will raise frequency. And bunching up air makes its mas//density larger, so in a part of the vocal tract where air moves a lot, constricting raises mass! So making a constriction increases mass and increases stiffness. 

But be careful!!!! This doesn’t mean that constrictions have no effect on frequency!!! Why? Because the parts of a vibrating medium that moves the most alternate with those that compress/uncompress the most!

shapes.text: Where were you a year ago?
My favorite experiment to show how complex speech is!!!!!
Back to AI: We will build an NN that will be trained on your Formants and will decide which vowel is being spoken
2 inputs → hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons → 5 outputs. No activation functions.

speakerNotes: A purely linear feed-forward network: 2 inputs, hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 output neurons, one per word.

shapes.text: Input (320, 2000). Every edge gets a random weight: blue positive, orange negative.

speakerNotes: Before training, every weight is a random number between −1 and 1.

shapes.text: The input flows forward, layer by layer. At the output: a distribution over the five words.

speakerNotes: Plays automatically in Slide Show and loops until you advance: dots carry the input forward, layer by layer; the output distribution [.5, .1, .1, .1, .2] appears; then the smiley.

shapes.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
 
# purely linear: 2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5
net = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False),  # 2 in → 3 out
    nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False),  # 3 in → 2 out
    nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False),  # 2 in → 4 out
    nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False),  # 4 in → 5 out
)
Declaration only, no training. bias=False keeps every layer purely linear, as in the picture.

speakerNotes: nn.Linear(in, out) holds an out × in weight matrix; bias=False removes the bias so each layer is a pure linear map.
